title: The Longest Necklace
subtitle: Why hasn't my Spirit Shell cracked yet?

items.text: The Longest Necklace
Lakeside
The stillness of the girl sitting in front of her contrasts with the rush of her arrival.
The lake lies quiet, holding a long, wordless note.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Miss Barcarola.
She pauses.
Her shell necklace hangs low. Her fingers run over its ridges again and again, finding deep and familiar grooves.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I remember you once said that you made the decision to leave your home all by yourself.
The ocean breeze swept across the deck that night as three girls shared secrets. Some kept theirs close; others let them drift.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: What did that feel like?
Faced with the calm and direct question, Barcarola allows herself to slip into memory.
She remembers when she chose to leave, standing in the plaza of Cremona, looking out toward the river, picturing the open sea beyond.
A white dove took flight, skimming past rooftops. By the time it flapped again, she felt she was already aboard.
Wind in her hair, heart soaring.
She had never imagined someone would ask her this. Perhaps to everyone else, the answer seemed obvious: a daring musician who sailed the waves should be fearless.
But her friend is from a world so different from her own. The answer she gives now must feel just as strange.
She hesitates. The moment hangs like the seconds before a symphony.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: It was what I wanted. I felt ... happy.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: In Cremona, all anyone could ever talk about and play was the violin. I didn't want to hear just one instrument my whole life.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I wanted to go everywhere, to find every instrument in the world, to hear them, to play them.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: That was my dream, and it still is.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I think "home" means something different to everyone.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: Cremona means something else to me now than it did then.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I do miss it sometimes.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: You could say it was only after leaving Cremona that I came to miss it at all.
Fatutu slinks her head into her shoulders.
Her shells are clinking between her fingers.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: You're right.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: We lived on our island, knowing nothing of the world beyond.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: And because of that, we never wondered what the outside was like. We were content with what was in front of us.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: The Nukutai don't stay away from home for long. We only ever set one course.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Maybe ... maybe it does mean something different. For us, it was the thing we were most afraid of losing, afraid of drifting away from it—never to see it again.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: Tutu?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: When we went out to sea, when we fished or planted, we only ever dealt with our own kin.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: We never trusted the merchants we traded with. They were always outsiders to us.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Then, when the island sank, we felt we had to trust, but we trusted the wrong people, and we lost our way.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I started doubting things the moment I stepped on that ship.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I remember. You were already starting to think maybe the outside world wasn't as scary as they said?
She nods almost imperceptibly.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I saw how the crew would cry out to one another, their faces so full of joy, like how Nukutai smile after the trade season.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I saw that girl—the other musical girl from the suitcase. She had her own ship. She stood there so proud, so striking.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: And then I saw you, Barcarola.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: People boarded the "Free Breeze" from all over the world, and they'd all stop to listen to your music.
Her words ring with so much sincerity that the musician can't quite bring herself to face her friend.
Fatutu looks out over the lake, in a stare that feels calm but tangled, like a knotted rope that's come loose, only to twist again.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Then I thought, if this world is really so full of hate and despair, why is everyone here so happy?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: And if we were wrong, and the world wasn't cruel, why did it swallow our island whole?

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I don't think it was anyone's fault. We just lived through a storm the likes of which no one's ever seen.
A storm that dragged nearly everyone into the depths, without mercy.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: When I first left, all I really wanted was to see what instruments people in other lands played and what kind of music they made.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: But before I could even find those instruments, I saw the passengers instead. And I saw that they were happy.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I also noticed that so often their first requests were to ask me to play something from their homeland.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: Sometimes it brought them comfort; sometimes it didn't.
She remembers those passengers, caught in moments of joy, followed by long, aching silences.

items.speaker: Barcarola
items.text: I realized then that there is no one in the world who is truly happy all the time. We all carry a little regret and a little sadness inside of us.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: You're right.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: That's something you only understand once you've set sail beyond your own shores.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Even so, knowing all this ...

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: We paid too high a price.
She lifts her shell necklace. Each piece a different shape, worn smooth by time.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: In Nukutaeao, when you trust someone, you carefully pick out a shell, polish it with care, and add it to their necklace.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: You can tell who is the most loved by who has the longest necklace.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: It would trail to their ankles, then wrap around their neck—once, twice, three times over.
She has one of those long shell necklaces, a symbol of the trust from the Nukutai.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I always dreamed of having the longest necklace.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: And we'd always ... always be in Nukutaeao, with my brother, Toa, and Selone.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: We'd always be there together.
She holds her head steady, as if trying to keep her gaze from falling into the deep water ahead.
Until at last she can't carry the weight anymore. She folds at the waist, falling like a wilting leaf.
She buries her face in her hands and trembles.
Tears stream out through her fingers, falling one by one into the lake.
It becomes a deep and sorrowful sob.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I always feared what my brother told me, that if we stayed away from home too long, the shells would crack and never be whole again.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: He's gone now. Toa's gone. We left Nukutaeao. And these shells ... they're still whole.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Kamuta ... brother ... I ... I wish more than anything that what you said was true.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I really, really do wish it were.
